toc.title: Crying is an action, not a state
Rage and panic are frozen fight and flight
Why crying sometimes doesn't bring relief

blocks.p: Where does crying fit on the Polyvagal ladder? It's a question I get, and the short answer is that it doesn't, at least not as a state. But it connects to the states in a really important way, especially to freeze.

blocks.h: Crying is an action, not a state

blocks.p: Crying is an action. It's a behavior, not a state, so it isn't on the ladder. The better question is which state it comes from.

I associate crying with release. It has to be a self-regulatory process. We feel better after a good cry. We tense up, and then we release, and our breathing spontaneously shifts. So I think crying is an impulse to self-regulate, or ideally it is. It's a way of climbing up the Polyvagal ladder.
And I think it comes from freeze. Some amount of frozen sympathetic activation (it doesn't have to be a ton) is being released through crying. It's releasing something that was once withheld.

blocks.h: Rage and panic are frozen fight and flight

blocks.p: To see why crying sometimes doesn't feel like release, it helps to know what's frozen.
Anger is just fight activation, basically. Anxiety comes from flight. Remember, sympathetic activation can have a flight or a fight flavor. That's the basic state activation.
But freeze is the combination of dorsal and sympathetic: shutdown plus flight or fight.

ul: When shutdown immobilizes flight, that's panic. Immobilized anxiety.
When shutdown immobilizes fight, that's not just anger. That's more like rage. Immobilized anger.

blocks.p: Immobilized anger just spins. It's bigger. It's not "I tell somebody off and I feel better." So rage is frozen fight activation, and panic is frozen flight activation.

When a fight-flavored freeze, a freeze with more fight in it, tries to release, it comes out as rage. Big, explosive. Stuff gets destroyed. Relationships get destroyed. People call it blackout anger: "I don't remember what happened. I blacked out." That's not just anger. To me, that's freeze, flavored by fight. Panic would be the flight-flavored freeze.

Some of my teenage clients, when they obviously needed to cry, I'd say, "It's okay to cry." And they'd say, "No, you don't understand. When I cry, I black out, stuff gets destroyed, and I don't know what happened." That's not just crying. It's not just releasing freeze for them. Their panic or rage comes up, it's too much, and they end up going right back down into their freeze state. It's not true release.

Think about someone who bullies or abuses. It's not that they're walking around irritable. There's a chronic, underlying rage, frozen into their system, which can explode at any moment. Not just anger, but a rage explosion.

blocks.h: Why crying sometimes doesn't bring relief

blocks.p: So crying from freeze could be really helpful. Ideally it is: with lots of safety anchoring, we actually release whatever's inside of us.

But if safety isn't active enough, the body is still attempting to release frozen rage, frozen fight or flight, and without that safety it just explodes and comes right back into the system. It's explosion and then implosion. Out, and then right back in. The pain gets reinforced instead of released, and a lot of times we end up destroying stuff or hurting somebody or ourselves.

If you cry a lot, maybe so much that you think you'll never stop, it's okay. It's not a bad thing. It's pretty darn normal, I think, especially if you're stuck in freeze, and especially if it's the more intense kind of freeze, with frozen flight or fight that leans toward panic and rage.
It's not hopeless. It's not easy, but things can definitely get better. Here are two broad options.

This is the most important one, and it's foundational: practice feeling safe. You can do it in little moments. You don't need a thirty-minute meditation. Practicing safety in micro moments can go a long way.

I've worked with clients with really high, intense anxiety or panic, lots of fear. The ones who seem to get the most benefit aren't changing their thoughts or fighting their feelings. They accept that this is how it is right now, and that they need to feel safe. So they find ways to feel safe.

That can be as small and accessible as using whatever senses you have access to and mindfully experiencing safety. Smell, taste, touch, look at, or listen to something that helps you feel better than not. I don't mean go get high and escape your problems. I mean: what helps you feel actually calm? Not drug-induced calm, but actually calm. What helps you feel like you can breathe, or smile? What helps you slow down a little?
If there's a smell you like, go do it. Spend just a few seconds with it and notice how it feels inside. I'm willing to bet that when you do, you won't have as much freeze active in that moment.

Does it solve your problems? Heck no. This is a sustained practice. You have to build the strength of your safety state. I don't know any other way around it. Practice feeling safe, day in and day out, in little micro moments, until you can work your way up to something more, like a deeper meditation on safety. You might not be there yet, and that's okay. It's never really a process that ends. All of us should do this.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: The second avenue is more or less approachable depending on who you are and how much of this you've done. Here the focus isn't on feeling calm and grounded. The focus is on being more active and using the frozen flight or fight activation.

This only becomes accessible when you have enough safety in your system to not feel immobile. If you're in an immobilized panic attack, or a blackout rage where you're not thinking at all, I don't think this will be very helpful. It's for when you have at least a little mindfulness, a little self-compassion, and some interest in what you feel inside, along with mild to moderate defensive activation. Not full-on panic, but moderate anxiety. Not rage, but irritability, anger.

When you have that, move. Get up and use the defensive activation you have within. What does your body want to do? Squeeze? Pull? Push? Throw? Not at other people or any living things. Use it, as long as it's not out of control.

How much safety you need for that, I can't tell you. But you'll know, because you'll be at least a little curious. You won't be rejecting your feelings, at least not as much. Instead you might have enough safety to say, "Okay, I'm noticing some anger. Let me use this now, before it grows into a full-on rage." Or, "I can notice my anxiety escalating. Let me use this now and go for a walk, before this turns into an immobilized panic."

Ideally you listen to your body and do what it needs. If it needs to pull, pull. If it needs to push into your palms, do it. If you need to push against the wall, go ahead. That requires being able to recognize what feels better than not in the moment.
I'd recommend practicing both of these way ahead of time.

If you live in a freeze state, you probably chronically have at least a little panic or rage in your system, which you might feel as anxiety, anger, irritability, nervousness, or worry. When it's low like that, and you can notice it, that's a really good time to practice what movement feels good, or what lack of movement feels good. Maybe you want to lie down on the floor. You can do that too. What feels best?

Practice that well before you need it. Then, as your activation escalates into stronger anxiety or stronger anger, use what you already know works for you. You have to practice it ahead of time, and you have to practice feeling safe ahead of time too.

As you do this, the intensity and frequency of those bigger rages and full-on panics can soften. I can't guarantee it for you, obviously. But in my client work, and from the feedback I get from people in my community, as they do these things, they soften. They get easier and easier, and they don't have as much of a debilitating hold over you.

That's the foundational process, in broad strokes. Things can get more specific, but I hope this starts you thinking differently about what crying means to you, and what rage and panic mean to you, where they come from. Focus on the foundational, day-in, day-out habits: practicing safety in micro moments, and noticing defense in small doses when you can tolerate it.
